entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Johannes Ockeghem (c. 1410/1425 – February 15, 1497) was a towering figure of the Franco-Flemish School, whose innovative compositional techniques profoundly shaped the trajectory of music during the early Renaissance. Serving three successive French kings—Charles VII, Louis XI, and Charles VIII—he held esteemed positions, notably as *maître de chapelle* and treasurer at the French court, granting him considerable influence and resources in Tours and Paris. His prolific output, characterized by intricate counterpoint, rich textures, and expressive melodic lines, positioned him as a central bridge between the ars nova traditions of Guillaume Du Fay and the polyphonic mastery of Josquin des Prez, establishing a foundational idiom for the High Renaissance.

Ockeghem's compositional legacy includes 14 masses, 10 motets, and 20 chansons, showcasing a remarkable technical prowess. His *Missa prolationum* is a contrapuntal tour de force, written entirely in mensural canon, where all four voices derive from a single melodic line through different proportional time signatures, a feat of intellectual complexity. The *Missa cuiusvis toni* ("Mass in any mode") further demonstrates his ingenuity, designed to be sung in any of the church modes without alteration, pushing the boundaries of modal theory and practical performance. These works illustrate his profound understanding of musical structure and his willingness to experiment with form and texture, often employing a deep bass range that was novel for his era.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Johannes Ockeghem's sophisticated contrapuntal techniques and structural innovations significantly advanced Renaissance polyphony, directly influencing the next generation of composers, including Josquin des Prez, and setting new standards for the genre across Europe.
